video_caption: The video opens with a black screen displaying light green text: "How to Format an APA Style Paper using Word for Mac" followed by "Terrence D. Jorgensen Kennesaw State University." This title text fades out, and a blue book cover appears, gradually becoming clear. The book is titled "Publication Manual" (with "Publication" in white and "Manual" in large green font) "of the American Psychological Association" (white text), and indicates "Sixth Edition" with a green and yellow swirly logo in the top left corner. The book cover then fades out, replaced by a 3D animated blue letter "W" logo (representing Microsoft Word) that rotates and transforms on a black background. This logo disappears to reveal a vibrant purple, pink, and blue abstract Mac OS X desktop background with a "Mac OS X" information window open in the center. The desktop and info window briefly show, then the "Publication Manual" book cover slides back into view before quickly moving off-screen to the right as a Microsoft Word document window, with a white page and a grey/blue interface, slides in from the left to fill the screen. The narrator begins to speak as the Word window is displayed, demonstrating how to move the window by clicking and dragging its top title bar and how to resize it by clicking and dragging the lower-right corner. Finally, the narrator illustrates how to adjust the zoom percentage in the bottom right of the Word window, causing the document's content to scale larger.

The video opens with a computer screen displaying a larger Microsoft Word application window with a ribbon at the top, and a smaller, distinct Microsoft Word window overlaid in the center. An animated grey arrow points from the smaller window's "Home" tab to the larger window's "Home" tab, suggesting a comparison or transition. The smaller window then disappears, leaving the larger "Document1" Word window as the focus. The cursor is seen clicking through various tabs on the ribbon of the larger Word window, demonstrating different categories of tools: first "Document Elements" (0:06), then "Tables" (0:08), "SmartArt" (0:10), and "Review" (0:12), with the ribbon display changing to show relevant options for each. Finally, the cursor clicks the "Home" tab (0:14) to revert to basic formatting options. Subsequently, the cursor moves to the operating system's top menu bar and clicks "File" (0:21), revealing a dropdown menu with standard file management options such as "New Blank Document," "Save," "Print," and "Properties."

The video segment shows a screen recording of a user interacting with Microsoft Word on a macOS operating system. Initially, a blank Word document titled "Document1" is displayed. A mouse cursor navigates to the "File" menu in the top left corner of the screen and clicks it, opening a dropdown menu. The cursor then selects "Page Setup..." from this menu. A "Page Setup" dialog box appears, showing "Settings: Page Attributes" and options for "Format For", "Paper Size", and "Orientation". The user clicks the dropdown menu next to "Settings: Page Attributes" and selects "Microsoft Word". The dialog box content changes to "Settings: Microsoft Word" with options to "Apply Page Setup settings to: Whole Document". The cursor then clicks the "Margins..." button. A new "Document" dialog box opens with two tabs: "Margins" and "Layout". The "Margins" tab is active, displaying input fields for "Top", "Bottom", "Left", and "Right" margins, along with "From edge" settings for "Header" and "Footer". The user changes the "Top", "Bottom", "Left", and "Right" margin values to "1"" (1 inch) and the "Header" and "Footer" values to "0.5"" (0.5 inches). Finally, the cursor clicks on the "Layout" tab, which then displays layout-related settings for the document.

The video displays a computer screen showing the Microsoft Word application interface with a document open. A "Document" dialog box is centrally positioned on the screen, featuring two tabs: "Margins" and "Layout," with "Margins" currently selected. Within this dialog, there are sections for "Section start" (showing "New page" selected), and "Headers and Footers" which includes checkboxes for "Different odd and even" and "Different first page." Below these, "Vertical alignment" is set to "Top." A small preview of a document layout is visible on the right, and the setting "Apply to: Whole document" is selected. At the bottom of the dialog, there are buttons for "Defaults...", "Page Setup...", "Cancel," and "OK." The speaker instructs the viewer to check the "Different first page" checkbox (which is currently unchecked) and then to click "Defaults" rather than "OK" to save the preference for future documents. The video ends before the check box is clicked, but just as the speaker mentions clicking "Defaults."

The video displays a Microsoft Word interface on a Mac, showing a blank document titled "Document1." The top menu bar includes options like "Word," "File," "Edit," "View," "Insert," "Format," "Font," "Tools," "Table," and "Window." Below that, there's a ribbon with various formatting options, including font selection (Cambria (Body)), font size (12), and paragraph alignment tools. A horizontal ruler is visible above the blank white document area. At 0:05, the mouse cursor hovers over the left indent marker on the ruler, and a tooltip appears, labeling it "Left indent." The speaker explains that these arrows control where the text appears independently of the margins. The cursor then moves to the top menu bar, clicks on "Format," and a dropdown menu appears with options like "Font...", "Paragraph...", "Document...", "Columns," "Tabs," "Drop Cap," "Text Direction...", "Change Case...", "AutoFormat...", and "Style...". At 0:05, "Font..." is selected from this dropdown menu, opening a "Font" dialog box. Inside the dialog, "Cambria (Theme Body)" is highlighted under "Font," and "Regular" is selected under "Font style," with "12" selected for "Size." The speaker explains that this dialog allows for more precise control over text settings.

The video opens with a computer screen displaying a Microsoft Word document on what appears to be a Mac operating system, with a "Font" dialogue box open in the center, showing "Cambria (Theme Body)" as the current font, "Regular" style, and "Size: 12". The mouse cursor then navigates to the "Font" field within this dialogue box, where "Times New Roman" is typed, changing the selected font to "Times New Roman" with "Regular" style and "Size: 12". Subsequently, the mouse clicks the "Default..." button, prompting a small pop-up window to appear with the question: "Do you want to change the default font to (Default) Times New Roman? This change will affect all new documents based on the NORMAL template." The "Yes" button is clicked, closing the pop-up and the "Font" dialogue box, revealing the main Word document window with "Times New Roman" and "12" now displayed in the font and size selection dropdowns on the toolbar. The mouse then moves to the top menu bar, clicks "Format," and from the dropdown menu, selects and clicks "Paragraph...". This action opens a "Paragraph" dialogue box, showing the "Indents and Spacing" tab active, with settings such as "Alignment: Left", "Indentation: Left 0", "Right 0", "Special: (none)", "Spacing: Before 0 pt", "After 0 pt", and "Line spacing: Single" visible.

The video displays a computer screen showing a Microsoft Word document titled "Document1" open in a macOS environment. A "Paragraph" dialog box is superimposed on the document, featuring two tabs: "Indents and Spacing" (currently selected) and "Line and Page Breaks". Under the "Indents and Spacing" tab, the "Alignment" is set to "Left," and "Indentation" values for "Left" and "Right" are both "0." The "Special" indentation field is initially set to "(none)," and at 0:02, the mouse cursor clicks on its dropdown arrow, revealing options for "(none)," "First line," and "Hanging." The "Spacing" section shows "Before: 0 pt," "After: 0 pt," and "Line spacing: Single." A checkbox labeled "Don't add space between paragraphs of the same style" is unchecked. A preview of text formatting is visible at the bottom of the dialog box, which also contains "Tabs...", "Cancel," and "OK" buttons.

The video opens with a computer screen displaying a Microsoft Word document. A "Paragraph" dialog box is open in the center, with the "Line and Page Breaks" tab highlighted. Under "Pagination," the "Widow/Orphan control" checkbox is initially selected. The narrator explains that this feature is not required by APA style and often wastes space. The narrator then clicks the checkbox to uncheck "Widow/Orphan control" and proceeds to click the "OK" button at the bottom right of the dialog box. The dialog box closes, revealing a blank Word document. The mouse cursor then moves to the top menu bar and clicks on "View." A dropdown menu appears, and the cursor highlights "Header and Footer" before the video ends.

The video segment shows a computer screen displaying a Microsoft Word document titled "Document1" with the "Header and Footer" tab selected on the ribbon. Initially, a blinking text cursor is present in the document's header area. The mouse cursor then demonstrates how to switch between the header and the main document text by double-clicking outside the header (activating the main text area) and then inside the header (activating the header area again). The "Header and Footer" tab remains highlighted. Following this, the mouse cursor moves to the "Insert" section within the "Header and Footer" ribbon and clicks on the "Page #" icon (a small calendar-like icon with a '5' on it). After clicking, the letter "R" is typed into the header of the document.

The video opens with a Microsoft Word document titled "Document1" on what appears to be a Mac operating system. The "Header and Footer" tab is currently active, displaying various options like "Header," "Footer," "Page #," and "Time." In the header section of the document, the text "Running head:" is typed. A cursor blinks after the colon, and a page number '1' is initially visible but not yet aligned. Following an instruction, the tab key is pressed, which moves the page number '1' to the far right margin of the document. The video then briefly highlights the right tab stop on the ruler at the top of the screen, confirming its alignment with the right margin. Subsequently, the text "ALL CAPS" is typed into the header, appearing after "Running head:" and before the page number '1', resulting in the full header "Running head: ALL CAPS 1". The entire header text is then selected, turning blue, and the ribbon interface briefly switches to the "Home" tab, showing "Times New Roman" as the selected font and "12" as the font size.

The video displays a Microsoft Word document, likely an older version for Mac, with a blank page in a window titled "Document1". The document initially shows a left-aligned header "Running head: ALL CAPS" and a right-aligned page number "1" at the top of the white page. The cursor blinks in the main body of the text, then moves down the page as if the "Enter" key is pressed multiple times. Subsequently, the text "Title: Subtitle" is typed, and then centered on the page by clicking the "Center Text" button in the "Paragraph" section of the ribbon, which briefly highlights in light blue. Following this, "Name" is typed and centered below "Title: Subtitle", and finally, "Institution" is typed and centered below "Name", all appearing in a standard black font.

In a Microsoft Word document on a Mac interface, the video demonstrates inserting page breaks and formatting text. Initially, text including "Running head: SUBTITLE" and "Title: Subtitle," "Name," "Institution" is visible. The user clicks "Insert" in the menu bar, then selects "Break," and finally "Page Break," causing the original text to disappear and a new blank page to appear. Subsequently, the word "Abstract" is typed and centered at the top of the newly created second page. Another page break is inserted through the "Insert" menu, leading to a third blank page where "Title: Subtitle" is centered at the top. The user then positions the cursor, highlights the left alignment button, and points to the first-line indent marker on the ruler, explaining that the abstract is the only paragraph in a manuscript that does not have a first-line indent.

The video segment shows a user interacting with a Microsoft Word document to edit headers. Initially, the first page's header displays "Running head: ALL CAPS" and the page number "1". The user highlights the text "ALL CAPS" along with the page number "1" (excluding "Running head:") and then right-clicks to select "Cut" from a context menu, making the highlighted text disappear. The view then scrolls down to a second page, whose header is empty. The user right-clicks in the empty header of the second page and selects "Paste" from the context menu, causing the text "ALL CAPS" and the automatically updated page number "2" to appear. The audio reinforces checking that the font remains Times New Roman 12-point. The video then briefly shows the header of the second page where the text "ALL CAPS" is initially centered, but after a quick transition, the header of the second page shows "ALL CAPS" now flush left with the page number "3", indicating a further automatic update and alignment adjustment.

The video segment showcases a user demonstrating how to format a "References" page in Microsoft Word. Initially, the user inserts a page break by navigating to "Insert" in the menu bar, then selecting "Break" and "Page Break." This action moves the content to a new page, displaying "ALL CAPS" and the word "References" centered, along with the page number '4'. Next, the user centers the "References" title using the "Center Text" icon in the toolbar and then adjusts it back to left alignment. After a slight zoom and a change in the document name to "Document1," the user demonstrates how to create a hanging indent. They first attempt to drag the hanging indent marker on the ruler bar. Then, they go to "Format" in the menu bar, select "Paragraph," open the "Indents and Spacing" tab, and choose "Hanging" from the "Special" dropdown menu under "Indentation," setting it to 0.5 inches before clicking "OK." Finally, a sample reference entry appears, "Name, A. B., & Second, C. D. (YEAR). Article title. Journal Title, vol #, page-page." (Name, A. B., & Second, C. D. (YEAR). Article title. Journal Title, volume number, page-page.), correctly formatted with a hanging indent, while the narrator advises consulting "the APA manual for details about how to properly format."

The video displays a computer screen showing a Microsoft Word document with a sample APA-style citation under a "References" heading. The citation includes "Name, A. B. & Second, C. D. (YEAR). Article title. Journal Title, vol #, page-page." The narrator explains the need for an en dash. The mouse cursor moves to the top menu bar, clicks "Insert," and from the dropdown, selects "Symbol" and then "Advanced Symbol..." A "Symbol" window appears, and the narrator clicks the "Special Characters" tab. In the list of special characters, "En Dash" is highlighted, and the narrator clicks "Insert," placing an en dash between "page" and "page" in the document. The narrator then opens the "Keyboard Shortcut..." option within the "Symbol" window, which reveals a "Customize Keyboard" dialog box. This box shows that the default shortcut for an En Dash is "Command + Numpad –" (Command + Numpad minus sign). The narrator then demonstrates creating a new shortcut by pressing "Command + -" (Command + hyphen) and clicking "Assign" in the "Customize Keyboard" dialog box.

The video displays a Microsoft Word document on a macOS operating system. The document contains the text "ALL CAPS" in the upper left corner and "References" centered below it. Further down, a sample reference format is visible: "Name, A. B., & Second, C. D. (YEAR). Article title. Journal Title, vol #, page-page. -". The cursor is initially at the end of this line. As the speaker explains different types of hyphens, a regular hyphen is typed, followed by two hyphens which then automatically transform into an en dash, and then three hyphens which transform into an em dash. The speaker emphasizes that each dash serves a specific purpose in APA style. The segment then focuses on demonstrating how to manually generate an en dash. The existing "page-page" text in the reference format is selected and deleted. The speaker types "page " followed by a single hyphen and then " page". As a space is typed after the second "page", the hyphen automatically converts into an en dash, connecting the two "page" words without spaces. The speaker concludes by reminding the viewer to remove any unnecessary spaces created during this process.

The video segment opens with a clear shot of a book cover, primarily blue with green text that reads "Publication Manual of the American Psychological Association" and "Sixth Edition" at the top. At the 00:17 mark, the scene transitions to a white title slide overlaid on a corner of the book cover. This slide displays the maroon title "Getting Started in APA Style," followed by "Terrence D. Jorgensen, Laboratory Coordinator, Psychology Department, Kennesaw State University" in black text. Below this, "Reference material: American Psychological Association. (2010). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association (6th ed.). Washington, DC: Author." is visible. The scene then transitions back to the blue book cover at 00:25, but now with new, prominent green text overlaid on it, stating "How to Format an APA Style Paper using Word for Mac." Finally, at 00:29, the screen becomes black, displaying the same green text: "How to Format an APA Style Paper using Word for Mac" and below it, "Terrence D. Jorgensen, Kennesaw State University."
